headings.title: Introduction to Uterine Abnormalities
headings.content: Uterine abnormalities encompass a broad spectrum of structural and anatomical variations of the uterus that can significantly impact a woman's reproductive health, menstrual cycle, and obstetric outcomes. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these conditions is vital because they are frequently encountered in gynecological and obstetric clinical settings across the country. Uterine abnormalities are broadly classified into two main categories: congenital malformations, which arise during fetal development due to the failure of the Müllerian ducts to properly form, fuse, or resorb, and acquired structural abnormalities, which develop later in life due to pathological processes, trauma, or hormonal imbalances. These anatomical deviations can present asymptomatically or manifest as severe dysmenorrhea, abnormal uterine bleeding, recurrent pregnancy loss, and infertility. Nurses play a frontline role in recognizing the symptoms, supporting diagnostic investigations, and providing compassionate care to women facing the physical and psychological burdens of these conditions. A strong foundation in the anatomy and physiology of the female reproductive system allows nurses to better educate patients, demystify medical jargon, and advocate for comprehensive reproductive healthcare services within the Nigerian healthcare framework.

headings.title: Embryology and Congenital Uterine Malformations
headings.content: Congenital uterine malformations result from disruptions in the normal embryological development of the female reproductive tract, specifically involving the paramesonephric or Müllerian ducts. During embryonic life, these paired ducts must undergo three critical phases: organogenesis, fusion, and resorption of the median septum to form a single, unified uterine cavity, cervix, and upper vagina. When any of these steps are arrested or impaired, various anomalies occur, classified by the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM). Class I involves Müllerian agenesis or hypoplasia, such as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. Class II represents a unicornuate uterus, caused by the arrested development of one duct. Class III consists of a uterus didelphys, resulting from a complete lack of fusion of both ducts, leading to two separate uteri and cervices. Class IV is a bicornuate uterus, characterized by partial fusion of the upper segments. Class V is a septate uterus, where fusion occurs normally, but the resorption of the intervening septum fails. Class VI includes arcuate uteri with a mild indentation at the fundus, and Class VII comprises diethylstilbestrol (DES)-related anomalies. Recognizing these embryological origins helps nursing students comprehend why patients with congenital malformations may also present with concurrent renal anomalies, given the close embryological development of the urinary and reproductive tracts.

headings.title: Acquired Structural Abnormalities
headings.content: Unlike congenital malformations that are present from birth, acquired structural abnormalities of the uterus develop over a woman's lifetime due to various pathological, inflammatory, or traumatic events. The most prevalent acquired anomalies include uterine fibroids, also known as leiomyomas or myomas, which are benign monoclonal tumors arising from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. Fibroids are classified based on their location within the uterine wall: intramural, subserosal, or submucosal, with submucosal fibroids having the most direct impact on the endometrial cavity. Another common acquired condition is endometrial polyps, which are localized overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma projecting into the uterine cavity. Intrauterine adhesions, commonly referred to as Asherman syndrome, develop as a result of trauma to the basal layer of the endometrium, most frequently following dilation and curettage (D&C) procedures performed after postpartum hemorrhage or elective termination of pregnancy. Adenomyosis is yet another acquired condition characterized by the benign invasion of endometrial tissue into the myometrium, causing diffuse or focal uterine enlargement. Additionally, retained products of conception and chronic endometritis represent acquired conditions that distort normal uterine architecture. Nurses must assess patients for risk factors such as parity, age, and history of intrauterine procedures to aid in early identification.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of uterine abnormalities directly dictates the clinical manifestations experienced by patients. When structural anomalies such as submucosal fibroids, polyps, or a septate uterus alter the contour or vascular supply of the endometrial cavity, normal implantation and sloughing are compromised. This often leads to abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), manifesting as heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), intermenstrual bleeding, or prolonged menses. Mechanical distortion can also impair the capacity of the myometrium to expand normally during pregnancy, resulting in recurrent miscarriage, second-trimester pregnancy loss, intrauterine growth restriction, malpresentation, and preterm labor. Furthermore, conditions like adenomyosis and deep intramural fibroids alter uterine contractility and cause ischemic changes, leading to severe dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. Some congenital anomalies, such as an obstructed hemivagina in association with a unicornuate uterus and renal anomaly (OHVIRA syndrome), can cause severe acute pelvic pain, hematocolpos, and dysmenorrhea shortly after menarche due to trapped menstrual blood. Nurses must recognize these clinical signs and conduct thorough pain and bleeding assessments to help differentiate uterine abnormalities from other pelvic pathologies.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Imaging Techniques
headings.content: Accurate diagnostic evaluation is essential for distinguishing between congenital malformations and acquired structural uterine abnormalities, as treatment strategies differ greatly. The diagnostic workup typically begins with a thorough patient history and physical examination, followed by imaging modalities. Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) is the first-line imaging technique used in clinical practice due to its non-invasive nature, accessibility, and high resolution for visualizing the myometrium and endometrium, helping to identify fibroids, polyps, and adenomyosis. However, TVUS may have limitations in differentiating between certain congenital anomalies, such as a bicornuate versus a septate uterus. To overcome this, saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) is frequently utilized, where sterile saline is instilled into the uterine cavity during ultrasound to better delineate intracavitary lesions like polyps and submucosal fibroids. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is considered the gold standard non-invasive imaging modality for mapping complex congenital uterine malformations and accurately evaluating adenomyosis due to its superior soft-tissue contrast. Hysteroscopy remains the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic tool for direct visualization of the intrauterine cavity, allowing the clinician to inspect and simultaneously treat conditions like adhesions, polyps, and small submucosal fibroids. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is also commonly used in fertility evaluations to assess tubal patency and uterine cavity contour.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: The management of uterine abnormalities depends on the specific diagnosis, the severity of symptoms, the patient's age, and her future reproductive desires. Medical management is primarily aimed at controlling symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and tranexamic acid are used to manage primary dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding. Hormonal therapies, including combined oral contraceptives, progestins, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, can help reduce fibroid size and control bleeding temporarily, though they do not correct underlying structural defects. Surgical interventions are required for definitive treatment or to restore reproductive capability. Hysteroscopic surgery is the preferred minimally invasive approach for resecting submucosal fibroids, endometrial polyps, and intrauterine adhesions (adhesiolysis), as well as for performing hysteroscopic metroplasty to correct a uterine septum. Laparoscopic or abdominal approaches are utilized for myomectomy, treatment of severe adenomyosis, or open metroplasty (such as the Strassman procedure for bicornuate uteri). Hysterectomy remains a definitive surgical option for symptomatic patients who have completed childbearing and do not respond to conservative measures. Nurses must provide comprehensive perioperative care, manage pain, monitor for postoperative hemorrhage, and offer emotional support.

headings.title: Impact on Fertility and Pregnancy Outcomes
headings.content: Uterine abnormalities can profoundly impact a woman's fertility and pregnancy outcomes, creating significant clinical challenges for obstetricians and midwives. Congenital malformations like a septate or bicornuate uterus reduce the functional endometrial surface area and possess abnormal vascularity, which impairs embryo implantation and early placental development. This significantly increases the risk of first- and second-trimester miscarriages, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), and preterm labor. Acquired abnormalities such as submucosal fibroids and large endometrial polyps act similarly to natural intrauterine contraceptive devices, physically obstructing embryo implantation or causing localized endometrial inflammation. Furthermore, anatomical distortion can lead to fetal malpresentations—such as breech or transverse lie—necessitating a higher rate of Cesarean delivery. For women undergoing assisted reproductive technologies (ART), uncorrected uterine abnormalities can drastically lower implantation and live birth rates. Nurses must be equipped to provide specialized antepartum monitoring, educate pregnant patients on warning signs of preterm labor, and offer sensitive psychological support to women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss due to uterine factors.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care and patient education are paramount in managing patients with uterine abnormalities, particularly within the diverse sociocultural context of Nigeria where reproductive health carries significant emotional and marital weight. Nurses hold the responsibility of performing holistic assessments, which include taking detailed menstrual and obstetric histories, assessing pain scores, and screening for psychological distress related to infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. Patient education must focus on explaining the specific diagnosis in clear, culturally sensitive language, outlining the rationale for diagnostic tests such as ultrasound or hysteroscopy, and discussing treatment options. For patients undergoing medical management, nurses must educate them on potential drug side effects and adherence. In the perioperative period, nursing interventions include monitoring vital signs, assessing vaginal bleeding, managing postoperative pain, and reinforcing warning signs that necessitate immediate medical attention. Furthermore, because infertility and pregnancy loss can lead to profound stigma, anxiety, and depression in many Nigerian communities, nurses must provide empathetic counseling, offer referrals to support groups, and ensure holistic care that addresses both the physical and emotional wellbeing of the patient.
